title: Why Do 91% of Us Have Grey Hair by 65?
description:
Why does hair turn grey? Melanocyte stem cells in the hair follicle stop moving and get stuck, so fewer colour cells make melanin, a finding from a 2023 study in mice.

Sources:
https://www.livescience.com/health/ageing/why-does-hair-turn-gray
https://www.npr.org/2023/04/21/1171110131/gray-hair-stem-cells-reversible

Animated in the Napkin Sketch style.
pinned_comment: If scientists could unstick those cells, would you keep your grey or go back?
script: Your grey hairs start with stuck cells, tiny ones, at your roots. Hair gets its colour from melanin, a pigment made by cells called melanocytes. They sit at the bottom of each follicle, and inject colour as the hair grows. But those cells need replacing, and that's the job of stem cells. In mice, scientists found these stem cells commute, moving up and down the follicle. Moving is how they get the signal to make colour. But as hair ages, more of them stop. They get stuck in a spot called the bulge. In plucked mouse hair, stuck cells jumped, from fifteen percent to nearly fifty. Stuck cells can't make new colour cells. Less melanin means grey, no melanin means white. By your early sixties, about ninety-one percent of people have some grey. So if scientists could unstick those cells, would you keep your grey, or go back?
key_facts: Melanin made by melanocytes at the base of the follicle gives hair its colour (Live Science)
2023 Nature study: melanocyte stem cells migrate up and down the follicle in mice, and with age more get stuck, unable to mature (Live Science, NPR)
Stem cells lodged in the follicle bulge rose from 15 percent to nearly 50 percent in repeatedly plucked mouse hair (NPR)
Less melanin gives grey hair, no melanin gives white (Live Science, citing the Library of Congress)
By age 61 to 65, 91% of people show some greying (Melissa Harris, UAB, in Live Science)
